transcript.text: induction hob keeps turnin off after 5-10 mins on high, have to keep restartin it. drives me nuts. any1 know y?

That's annoying, but it's usually one of a few common things, and most are easy to fix:

1. It's the boost/max setting timing out (most likely)
Many induction hobs only allow the top power level (often "P", "B" or "9") for a limited time, typically 5-10 minutes, then automatically drop or switch off. That's a built-in safety feature, not a fault. Check your manual for "boost" or "automatic switch-off" times. Using a level just below max usually avoids it.

2. Overheating protection
The electronics underneath have a cooling fan. If the hob gets too hot it shuts off to protect itself. Check that:
• There's a ventilation gap under the hob (nothing stored tight against it in a drawer below, and no blocked vents)
• The fan is actually running (you should hear a whirring when it's on)
• It isn't installed directly above an oven without proper ventilation

If it used to work fine and only recently started doing this, a failing fan is a strong suspect.

3. The pan
• Too small for the zone, warped, or not fully magnetic, so the hob loses detection
• Very thin pans can overheat fast and trigger the temperature sensor
• Test: a fridge magnet should stick firmly to the base

4. Something on the controls
Liquid, steam, a boiled-over spill, or a utensil resting on the touch panel can make it think a button's been pressed and shut off. It often beeps when this happens.

5. Power management setting
Some hobs have a power limiter (set during installation) that cuts zones when total power demand is too high, especially if you're using several zones at once.

Quick tests:
• Try one pan on a lower setting (e.g. 7-8) for 15+ mins. If it stays on, it's the boost timer.
• Does it show an error code when it cuts out? If so, tell me the code and brand and I can help decode it.
• Is it worse when multiple zones are on? That points to power management or overheating.

If it's overheating and the fan seems dead, that's one for an engineer, since there's mains electricity inside.

What brand/model is it? That'd help narrow it down.
Samsung. dont know the model and not looking under it. new drawer unit went in under it a month ago, cutouts only started after that. fan roars before it cuts out

That pretty much solves it. The new drawer unit is almost certainly blocking the hob's airflow, so it's overheating.

The fan roaring flat out right before the cutout is the giveaway. The fan is struggling to cool the electronics, can't, and the hob shuts itself off to protect itself. Timing matching the new drawers seals it.

Why it happens
Induction hobs need to pull in cool air and push out warm air underneath. Drawer units are often fitted tight up to the worktop, or the top drawer is full of stuff sitting right against the hob's underside, so the hot air just recirculates.

Things to check (no need to look under the hob itself)
• Top drawer contents: Is anything stacked high or touching the underside of the hob? Clear it out and try cooking on high. If it stops cutting out, that's your answer.
• Gap at the top: Most manufacturers want a clear air gap (often around 20mm or more) between the bottom of the hob and anything below it.
• Back of the unit: There usually needs to be a ventilation gap or opening at the back so warm air can escape. New units often have a solid back panel right up to the wall.
• Plinth/kickboard: Some installs need a vent there too.

Fixes
• Keep that top drawer shallow or empty, or fit a heat shield/divider panel with a gap above it (often sold as an induction hob protector board).
• Cut a vent slot in the back panel of the unit, or ask whoever fitted it to sort it. They should have followed the hob's installation clearances.
• Your hob's installation guide will list exact clearances. Search your model online; the model number is often on a sticker under the hob, but sometimes also on the warranty card or the original box/paperwork.

Don't just keep restarting it if you can help it. Repeated overheating isn't great for the electronics long term.

Try the empty drawer test first. That'll tell you in one cook.
